comment_content: This course covers introductory calculus. Topics include functions, limits and continuity, derivatives, applications of derivatives, and a brief introduction to integrals. Most of the semester focuses on differentiation, while integration is only covered near the end. The course is fairly standard and serves as a foundation for many quantitative courses later on.

comment_grading:
The grading scheme consists of 10% WeBWorK assignments, 35% midterm, and 55% final exam. The WeBWorK assignments are mainly based on completion and are an easy source of marks if you stay on schedule.
The course appears to use absolute grading rather than a strict curve. For reference, the midterm mean was 42.74 with a standard deviation of 17.90, while the final exam mean was 43.49 with a standard deviation of 18.40. I scored 86 on the midterm and 99 on the final exam, which were both the highest scores, and received an A+ for the course. Overall, the grading is straightforward.
comment_workload:
The workload is reasonable. Xueyang provides very detailed notes as well as problem sets for additional practice. The problem sets do not count toward the final grade, but they are extremely useful for exam preparation. Just make sure you understand all the examples in the notes and work through the problem sets carefully. That is usually enough preparation for the exams. 
One thing to be careful about is relying too heavily on past papers. The difficulty can vary significantly from year to year. I underestimated the midterm because I expected it to be similar to previous papers, and that turned out to be really wrong.

comment_content: MATH1013 is the standard first-year single-variable calculus course at HKUST, a core compulsory subject for most engineering, science and business students. Compared with the more theoretical MATH1023, it focuses on applied computation rather than rigorous proofs, serving as a beginner-friendly foundational math course for new undergraduates.
comment_teaching: he teaching team of MATH1013 is well-organised and highly student-oriented. Lecturers explain concepts clearly and break down intimidating calculus ideas into digestible steps. They place strong emphasis on intuition rather than dry formulas, carefully demonstrating how each computation rule works and warning students about common pitfalls. Lecture slides are well-structured, concise and easy to review after class.
comment_grading: An A grade requires fluency in nearly all computational techniques and firm conceptual understanding. A B is attainable if you master most question types, even with small gaps in advanced concepts. A C satisfies the minimum passing threshold and only demands competence in basic calculations. The overall failure rate is low.
comment_workload:
The workload of MATH1013 is **light-to-moderate** among HKUST core maths courses, and it is very manageable if you keep up weekly.
Weekly tasks include standard lecture viewing, tutorial preparation, and problem set completion. Assignments are not excessively long; most questions are repetitive practice problems designed to solidify calculation skills rather than trick students. The time commitment is roughly 3–5 hours outside lectures per week for an average student.

comment_content: MATH 1013 covers standard Calculus I topics, including functions, limits, continuity, derivatives, applications of derivatives, and basic integration. Most of the course is computational and problem-solving based, but some concepts require a bit more understanding, such as continuity, differentiability, Mean Value Theorem, L’Hôpital’s Rule, Riemann sums, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Overall, the content is quite manageable if you keep practicing. Stewart’s Calculus is more than enough for this course, and doing the relevant examples and exercises properly should prepare you very well for exams. The course is not conceptually too difficult, but careless mistakes can cost a lot, so accuracy matters.
comment_teaching: I did not attend any lectures, so I cannot comment too much on the live teaching quality. From what I heard and from the materials, the teaching pace seemed quite slow, especially for students who already had some calculus background. For me, self-studying from Stewart and practicing problems was more efficient.
comment_grading:
The grading is fair. The exams are not impossible or designed to trick students unfairly. If you do the homework seriously and, most importantly, finish all available past papers carefully, you should be well prepared.
The key is not only knowing the formulas, but also avoiding careless mistakes. Since the course is relatively standard, exam preparation is quite straightforward: understand the concepts, do past papers, check your mistakes, and repeat
comment_workload:
The workload is very light. Apart from online homework and exam preparation, there is not much regular pressure. The homework is manageable, and if you keep up with it, the course will not take much time weekly.
Overall, I would say this is a pretty easy course if you are disciplined. If you slack off until the last minute, it can still punish you, but if you consistently do Stewart + homework + past papers, getting into the A range is very realistic.

comment_content: The content of L01 is rigorous and theory‑driven, clearly designed for students intending to major in mathematics. Instead of focusing mainly on computational techniques, the course emphasizes logical reasoning, foundational concepts, and proof writing. Topics such as logic, set theory, injectivity/surjectivity, limits, continuity, differentiability, and the mean value theorem are treated with a level of depth that goes beyond standard introductory calculus. This approach builds strong mathematical maturity and prepares students well for higher‑level pure math courses. However, students expecting a more application‑oriented or formula‑driven calculus course may find the abstract style challenging.
comment_teaching: Dr. Cheng adopts a clear, structured, and concept‑focused teaching style. His lectures prioritize understanding over memorization, often explaining the motivation behind definitions and the logic behind proofs. The course environment encourages students to think critically and engage with the material at a deeper level. Office hours are generous and flexible, and the instructor seems approachable and supportive. The TAs also play an important role, especially in tutorials where students practice writing proofs and clarifying conceptual difficulties.
comment_grading: The grading scheme is heavily weighted toward the midterm and final exam (42% each), with written assignments making up the remaining 16%. The assignments emphasize clarity of reasoning and proof writing rather than routine calculations, which aligns with the course philosophy. The lowest homework score is dropped, which helps reduce pressure. Because the exams are long, closed‑book, and conceptually demanding, students need a solid grasp of the material rather than surface‑level familiarity. Overall, the grading is fair but challenging, rewarding students who genuinely understand the concepts.
comment_workload: The workload is moderate to heavy depending on your background. Students with strong mathematical foundations (e.g., HKDSE M1/M2 or prior exposure to proofs) will find the pace manageable, though still intellectually demanding. Those new to abstract reasoning may need to invest significant time outside class to digest the material. Homework assignments require careful writing and cannot be rushed. While there is no WeBWork component for L01, the depth of the written assignments and the conceptual nature of the exams mean consistent weekly effort is essential.
